blocks.text: HABAKKUK THE PROPHET (HABAKKUK 1:1) · TWO KINGDOMS
Habakkuk. He asked the LORD “how long?”, waited on his watch for the answer, and ended in a song.
SCRIPTURE CALLS
Prophet
ERA
Two kingdoms 930–586 BC
IN THE DAYS OF
No ruler named beside him
BOOK
Habakkuk
HOW THE WORD CAME
“The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see.”
THE CALL
How the word came
“The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see.” Much of the book is his own questions to the LORD and the LORD's answers. Habakkuk 1:1–2 Habakkuk 1:5 Habakkuk 1:12–13 Habakkuk 2:2

He waited for the answer like a watchman: “I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower”. He was told to write the vision down plainly “upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.” Habakkuk 2:1–3
Chapter 3 is “A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth”, with “Selah” in it and a note at the end for “the chief singer on my stringed instruments”. Habakkuk 3:1 Habakkuk 3:3 Habakkuk 3:19
THE MESSAGE
The word in its main themes
How long?
“O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!”
Habakkuk 1:2 (KJV) →
The Chaldeans raised up
“For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation”
Habakkuk 1:6 (KJV) →
Why the wicked over the righteous?
The just shall live by his faith
“though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.”
Habakkuk 2:3 (KJV) →
“but the just shall live by his faith.”
Habakkuk 2:4 (KJV) →
Five woes
“For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.”
Habakkuk 2:14 (KJV) →
“But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.”
Habakkuk 2:20 (KJV) →
Yet I will rejoice
“Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines”
Habakkuk 3:17 (KJV) →
“Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.”
Habakkuk 3:18 (KJV) →
THE WORD TO …
To whom the word was spoken
TO THE CHALDEAN
“Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee”
Habakkuk 2:8 (KJV) →
THE BOOK
The book of Habakkuk
1 Heading Habakkuk 1:1
2 How long? Habakkuk 1:2–4
3 The answer: the Chaldeans Habakkuk 1:5–11
4 The second question; the watchtower Habakkuk 1:12–2:1
5 The vision; the just shall live by faith; five woes Habakkuk 2:2–20
6 The prayer Habakkuk 3:1–19
WHERE THE NEW TESTAMENT QUOTES IT · 4
Each band joins a chapter of Habakkuk to the New Testament books quoting it (4 books).
HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
From the textScripture says nothing of Habakkuk outside his book. Habakkuk 1:1 Habakkuk 3:1
TRADITION SAYS

An angel carries “a prophet, called Habbacuc” by the hair of his head from Judea to Babylon to bring Daniel his dinner in the lions' den, and sets him back again. T. Witton Davies judged this episode a later addition to the story. Bel and the Dragon 1:33–39 [50] Who says so: Bel and the Dragon 33–39, an addition to Daniel in the Greek Bible, printed in the Apocrypha of the King James Version, Davies (1913) assumes a Hebrew text of about 136 BC, the Greek being later

The Greek heading of Bel and the Dragon says it was taken “From the prophecy of Hambakoum, son of Jesus, of the tribe of Levi.”[46] Who says so: The Septuagint's heading to Bel and the Dragon, as translated by A. B. Davidson (1896), In the Greek translation, which Davies (1913) holds later than a Hebrew original; no firmer date is given here

Habakkuk was of the tribe of Simeon. “It is said that when Jerusalem fell in 586 he fled to Ostracine on the borders of Egypt, but returned to his native place on the withdrawal of the Chaldeans … and died two years before the return of the exiles from Babylon. His tomb was pointed out in Keilah.”[46][50] Who says so: The Lives of the Prophets ascribed to Epiphanius, as summarised by A. B. Davidson (1896), Davidson calls the ascription to Epiphanius (bishop from AD 367) perhaps wrong; he does not date the work
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
Under Jehoiakim, as the Chaldeans rose
S. R. Driver (1891); A. B. Davidson (1896)

The Chaldeans are being raised up (Hab 1:6). Driver: “The prophecy may be assigned with great probability to the reign of Jehoiakim (B.C. 608-598)”. Davidson puts chapter 1:5–11 no earlier than the battle of Carchemish (“605 — 4”). Habakkuk 1:6 [3][46]
Late in Manasseh's reign
C. F. Keil (1868); Seder Olam, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1905)
Keil narrows the choice to Josiah's reign or “the closing years of Manasseh” and leans to Manasseh. The Seder Olam places Joel, Nahum and Habakkuk “in the reign of Manasseh.”[11][42]
IN SCRIPTURE
Every passage
CHAPTERS · 7
Habakkuk 1 Habakkuk 2 Habakkuk 3 Acts 13 Romans 1 Galatians 3 Hebrews 10
PASSAGES · 5
Habakkuk 1:1–3:19 Acts 13:40–41 Romans 1:17 Galatians 3:11 Hebrews 10:37–38
WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture gives no call, no family, no home and no king for Habakkuk.
Habakkuk 3 is set for music, but the text does not say Habakkuk was a Levite or a temple singer.
